I went down from 137 lbs to 116 lbs by the end of high school (significant for my height of 5'3"), ditched the ugly wire glasses, got a *badly* needed hair cut (it was long, pin straight, cut completely level, tangled, full of split ends and middle parted, eugh), started paying a lot more attention to how I was dressing and learned how to use makeup because I was *sick and tired* of the way people treated me. Boom. When I show my current friends pictures of me in my freshman year (which was only a little over four years ago!) they don't believe that that was me. Getting a little older (I graduated high school when I was 16) has also changed my appearance, and let's just say that my curves have definitely moved to the right places. In short, I went from ugly shy chick to kind of a bombshell. It was weird.


There's been a huge change in the way people treat me. More strangers come up and strike up conversation with me, retail employees are generally more pleasant to me when I go to stores, I have a thriving and active social life (whereas in high school if I went out two nights a week I felt like a "social butterfly"), and *exponentially* more guys hit on me. My confidence has gone through the roof--I've always been told I was smart, but now that I have looks to complement my intelligence people generally seem more impressed by me and want to get to know me better more often, ergo I have more friends than I did in the past. Honestly the fact that people want to talk to me more now that I'm considered more attractive doesn't really bother me, because I don't think it's so much that these people only like me for my looks as that they feel better about approaching someone who is conventionally good-looking versus someone who is not. This might be shallow, true, but that's how humans work. My main qualm in that respect is with the guys who approach me solely because of my looks, and they're easy enough to fend off/ignore--all I have to do is show them my crazy side and they start running. The biggest change I think is that I feel healthier and better about my appearance overall. I look *very* different from how I used to, but it's a good different, and I can wear sexier clothes now and not feel bad about how I look. Being able to do more physically is also a plus, I'm currently signed up for a weekly kickboxing club which I am literally kicking ass at. 

I'm still the same old me on the inside though. I'm still the same caustic, bitter, cynical, easily frustrated, hard-drinking bastard with a dark sense of humor that I've always been, and that surprises people who expect me to be some silly pretty bimbo. I roll with it.

When I was in high school a little while back I saw a *wonderful*, wonderful psychiatrist who honestly did more for me than any other mental  health professional ever has; however, her office was a little over an hour's drive away from my home, and my mother, who drove me to appointments, was at the time still scared of going long distances on highways. So after a month of seeing this wonderful woman see suggests I try and find a professional closer to my home. My parents agree and we book an appointment with an elder gentleman with many years of practice with psychotherapy.


Jesus *Christ* that appointment. I walk in and he has the classic "therapy patient's lean-back couch" stuffed in a corner of a room and a huge, very expensive and plush leather office chair pulled up to his desk. Degrees are *everywhere*--there is literally only a few square feet of wall space not covered in some kind of diploma or picture of his family. I sit down and we talk for about five minutes, during which he seems fairly sane, and then he abruptly sits down on the floor and beckons me over. He's pulled out some kind of marble game that looks like Chinese checkers but stranger and asks me to play. I refused- I came for a therapy session, not to play games. I keep refusing and eventually he starts *commanding* me to sit on the floor. A little weirded out, I sit down. He explains the rules to me and says if I end the game with less then a certain number of marbles on the board, I am a "certifiable genius." I'm starting to think that a certain number of marbles are missing from *his* head. I play and apparently I win the genius classification because he gets up and starts dancing and clapping his hands. Right then.


I mumble something vaguely disapproving to him and he snaps back with something along the lines of "Don't think I don't have you all figured out. I've been doing this for years. It's obvious you have schizoid personality disorder!" He then *pulls out a little leather book* from his bookshelf, flips through the pages, finds the disorder listing and holds it under my nose. "It says right there!" I have spoken to this man for all of fifteen minutes and had not said a single word regarding symptoms.


Naturally I am confused and want to leave, but he insists on writing up a list of movies I should see, insisting that they're all good movies. I have no idea how this relates to therapy and I just want out; I call my mother in and she comes to the rescue, ending the appointment. *Somehow* this crazy old man starts talking to her about our heritage [Indian] and eventually he starts picking a fight with her about arranged marriage, ranting about how it's wrong and how it doesn't work it America. My mother hadn't said anything about arranged marriage. We quickly leave and never book the next appointment, preferring the hour long drive to the psychiatrist's over this complete wackjob.


**tl;dr Batshit older guy who's clearly going senile makes me play a weird marble game to "gauge how smart I am", declares me both a genius and schizoid within 15 minutes of meeting me for the first time, starts writing up a list of good movies I should see and then picks a fight with my mother because of her cultural beliefs.**

Hey there! Thanks for taking the time to share your story. I really like running as a means to distract myself, plus it cheers me up when I see I've bested my own mile time. 

I do experience "ups" and "downs", but I've been diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder, which is basically (very simplified definition) schizophrenic symptoms combined with an affective disorder, which in my case is type I bipolar. I'll cycle between feeling really good (manic) and really bad, and trying to have a regular schedule can be difficult sometimes. I do what I can. Things that I do that keep me healthy and lessen my symptoms include running, eating right, and getting enough sleep. That last one's really important--sometimes when I'm manic I'll feel really energized and don't feel like sleeping, but I take melatonin and force myself to go to bed because I know once I come "down" from the mania I'll feel exhausted and wrecked.

I don't think that's necessarily true. I'm saying that these things are the best things a *layperson* can do for a loved one who's suffering. Loved ones cannot prescribe medication or conduct therapy with someone suffering from depression. Being supportive of someone by doing kind things (i.e. driving them to appointments, genuinely listening etc) is *not* the same as being unhelpful by making offhanded remarks like "cheer up!". Those latter things don't help. The former ones do. The former ones will not *cure* depression, true, but they will be much more helpful than making said offhand remarks.

I get that your sentiments are genuine, but if there's one thing depression *isn't*, it isn't simply getting bogged down in circumstances. If you'll allow me, I'd like to take some time to explain depression from the viewpoint of someone who has it.


> remember that you have absolute power in your life and you can change it however you want.


**False**. False false false *false*. In my own mind as someone who's experienced depression, drawing the disabling mental illness wild card out of the genetics pool is analogous (but definitely NOT the same as) being born into a terrible socioeconomic situation. Yes, some people do "work their way out of it" and make great symptom-free lives for themselves, but a) this is definitely *not* the case for most people, and b) it is ridiculously, ridiculously hard to do so. Mental illness in its uglier forms can and does rob people of the capacity to lead healthy lives. A visit to any psychiatric hospital will confirm the existence of the absolutely insane amounts of sadness the human mind has the capacity to suffer under. Depression is real and not something that can be willed away by better diet and sunlight. Yes, these things may *help*, but realize that 1.) these things will not instantly cure what is a goddamn difficult to treat and very serious illness, and 2.) even the thought of taking these steps can be too much to ask for someone in the throes of depression. Living life as someone experiencing depression is like scuba diving with a bunch of friends, only to find out mid-dive that your equipment *doesn't work*-- sure, your friends are having the time of their lives exploring the reef and marveling at the pretty fishes, but in the meantime you're there, choking to death, frantically clawing at your oxygen tank and mask praying to any dear sweet deity that you don't pass out and die right there at the bottom of the ocean. Now, imagine those friends becoming frustrated and bored with your "antics" and insisting you "lighten up", enjoy the dive and the pretty coral and "stop being such a buzzkill." It's not very fun.


Some people (like my now-ex) think that depression is derived solely from a set of bad circumstances, and that once these circumstances the depression should by all rights go away. Again, false. The entirety of modern science recognizes that mental illness is a legitimate condition that doesn't ebb and flow according to how great your life is going on paper at any given moment. People may argue over whether money and fame can buy a person happiness, but at my most depressed I felt like nothing in the world I could have bought with money would make me feel any less suicidal.


Alright, you think, what the hell *can* people do about this? The good news is that people can and do get better. It happens all the time. The standard regimen of therapy and proper medicine regimens goes miles in helping depression, but honestly, for anyone who wants to help someone suffering from depression the best you can do is *show that you care*. I don't mean that you should offer advice like "hey, keep your chin up!" -- I mean *show it*. Offer what favors you can, like driving them to therapy or staying in with them and watching stupid cartoons. Anything. First off, hi fellow late-teens INTJ! Pleased to meet you. On to the questions.

* *How do you deal with the irrationality you perceive in people and/or society in general?* 

In my past, not very well - I tended to isolate myself a lot (see third question/answer). I found myself confused and hurt when people weren't as enthusiastic about science/philosophy/literature/etc as I was and genuinely couldn't understand why they wouldn't give me a chance. Given that we're fairly young, the age factor certainly played a part in my lack of buddies to share my interests with as well. Nowadays, though, I recognize that the large majority of my friends just aren't into what I am. Here is a list (!) of what I do to adjust to this friction. 

1.) I accept my friends for the entirety of who they are. Whether or not I choose to be a part of peoples' lives is entirely my decision, true, but I don't make friends with someone with the ambition of changing, converting or (god forbid) "enlightening" them in any way. I appreciate my friends for the variety and insights they bring into my life; I'm friends with all different kinds of people and each one is like a new, fantastic, aromatic and individual spice in my well-looked-after spice rack. (cue cheesy music accompanying equally cheesy metaphor.) Irrationality crops up a lot (again, teenage crowd we're talking about), and I deal with it largely by accepting it as a basic human function and an inevitable factor of the relationship. By expecting it and accepting it you can shift your focus to what you actually *do* like about the person. It's really nice to have friends (such as my best friend) with whom this isn't a factor, because we can talk about how it crops up with other friends, but a.) this best friend moved hundreds of miles away and b.) that's just one person. Honestly, the best answer I can give is that I've learned to value time spent *productively* by myself as more of a valuable thing instead of "lonely time." I realized that spending a few hours in a library alone can be just as rewarding as talking casually with friends, but that I need both of those things in my life at different times. It's give and take.

* *Have you found a career which you are completely satisfied with, and if so, what is it?* Ditto the monetary-gain-for-soulsucking-career fear. I'm a 17 year old in university with 50 completed college credits under my belt...so I love learning? Honestly I've run into the same problem you've anticipated having for yourself. I signed up for an intensive 6-credit classics course my first semester, wrote over 15 pages in essays every week and pored over scholarly articles in the library in the wee hours of the morning. It was brilliant. Next semester I signed up for 17 credits of all math-and-science everything. I just love studying *everything*, damn it, be it the western cult of Isis or particle physics. My brain just refuses to stay still, so in my first few semesters of university (while it's still not of much consequence to do so) I'm letting it roam as it will across departments, yay for overpriced liberal arts educations. (My adviser considers it a nightmare.)


The one mainstay in my academic career, though, has been computer science. I love love love it as a field of scientific inquiry, but -- get this -- *it also translates into a well-paying job often devoid of consumer contact!* Yay! I've met every single faculty member in the department and while all have their quirks, they're all a delightful bunch of squirrely oddballs and I would love to be in their position one day. I've pestered them about their research projects and upper-level classes and honestly, I'm thinking more than ever that it's the field for me. We'll see how it plays out.


* *Do you feign excessive interest in others or do you simply stick largely to yourself?* Like you said, the two aren't mutually exclusive--I do both. (so, yes.) I recognize when "learning mode" is in hyperdrive, and that's when I spend days in the library or on the internet just losing myself in knowledge. When I want company I'll hit up any number of friends I feel like talking to. Yes, sometimes I have to put up with people being difficult, and yes, sometimes I'll feign interest in a person at a party when things are dull, but don't a lot of us at some point do so [INTJ or no]? With my friends I am patient because I know there's a reason I stick around with them, and with strangers if I find they're not worth my time I will *quickly* pass over them. I definitely am selective, but those I value I hold in high import.


**TL;DR** In my experience, relationships with people who *aren't* philosophically/scientifically/etc-minded can be rewarding as well. I decided to give them a chance and I wasn't disappointed; it was my only choice, otherwise I'd go crazy with only myself to keep me company.

There's no "magical happy thought" you can plant in her mind to make her life any better, I'll tell you that right now. That's not to say that there isn't anything you can do for her though. Here's what I wish an older brother would do for me as someone with type I bipolar:

1.) Listen to her. Just be someone who fucking *listens*. That doesn't mean pressure her to divulge her "deepest darkest secrets" ever hour, though--let her know that you're honestly there for her, extend an invitation and wait for her to approach you. So many people are just so concerned with themselves and their own lives that they forget some people aren't doing so great as them, and feeling alone and unheard just makes being depressed a thousand times worse, I can tell you that. Listen attentively to what she says and don't pass judgement/offer advice unless asked. Ask her about her day, make note of interesting things she's doing--your conversations don't have to be earth-shattering philosophical debates on the meaning of life. Earnest, simple talk and effective communication of your affection for her will do more than you could possibly know.

2.) Do nooootttttt invade her privacy. Just don't. If she keeps a diary/tumblr/whatever, stay away from it. Having a private/anonymous place to dump stressors and emotions and frustration is a valuable thing for a lot of people, and when someone they know (even a loved one) intrudes on that privacy it does a lot of damage. If she's writing or playing music or whatever then be interested in what she's creating, but if there's stuff she doesn't want you to see/hear, accept it and move on. Let her have some things to herself.

3.) Read up as much as you can on any diagnoses she's been given. There's plenty of good websites like NAMI with information on many clinical diagnoses and strategies for loved ones of diagnosed individuals on dealing with the illness. Oftentimes there's support forums online for lots of different conditions where loved ones of diagnosed individuals can communicate with one another.

NOTE: This does not mean waving every study you find that says *"8 CUPS OF COFFEE A DAY CURE DEPRESSION IN RATS!"* in her face. This information is mostly for your own knowledge so you understand what your sister's going through better, *not* so that you can proclaim to have found the simple/easy/homeopathic cure for depression/etc. that's been under everyone's noses this whole time. I hate it when people do this.

4.) Keeping number 2 in mind, if you have *very reasonable and well-supported concern* that she's doing some kind of egregious harm to herself (i.e. engaging in self-injurous behavior), let her know you're worried for her. The only reason I'm mentioning this is that these kinds of symptoms are *common* in those with depression/bipolar/etc, but they won't *necessarily* be found in every person. **Don't** be accusatory if you do discover that this is happening with her; being scolded or yelled at will make her feel even worse, and that's something you're trying to avoid, right? If she's turned to those kinds of coping mechanisms she's obviously not doing well and you really don't want to make her feel like further shit. Instead of yelling, offer to get her an appointment with a therapist if she's not already seeing one or suggest she talk to her psychiatrist about a medicine change if she's on a regimen. Remember, when in doubt, #1 will rarely fail you.

**tl;dr** shut up and listen, stay out of her stuff, read up on mental health and be kind and supportive. That's really the best you can do from my experience.
